overview.text: Released in 1915, D. W. Griffith’s epic film The Birth of a Nation follows two white families through the Civil War and Reconstruction, adapting Thomas Dixon Jr.’s novel The Clansman. It presents Reconstruction from a Confederate-sympathetic viewpoint, relies on degrading racist stereotypes of Black people, and portrays the Ku Klux Klan as heroic. Those portrayals are racist distortions, not reliable history. The film’s scale and filmmaking helped establish feature films as a major form of popular entertainment, while its popularity also helped the revived Klan attract supporters. The NAACP protested and campaigned against its screenings, making the film significant both in cinema history and as an example of media shaping public memory.

key_facts.text: Griffith premiered the film in Los Angeles in February 1915; it was based on Thomas Dixon Jr.’s novel The Clansman.
Its plot links two white families to a Confederate-leaning account of the Civil War and Reconstruction.
The film vilifies Black people through racist stereotypes and glorifies the Ku Klux Klan; the NAACP organized protests and sought to stop screenings.
Its filmmaking and popularity helped elevate feature films, but the revived Klan also used the movie’s success as a recruiting tool.
